businesses.pitch: A team of coders and designers who build phone apps for clients and for themselves.
businesses.earns: Companies pay you to build their apps, and your own apps earn money from downloads and small in-app purchases.
businesses.costs: Salaries for coders and designers, powerful computers, cloud servers that run the apps, and adverts for new launches.
businesses.risks: A new app can flop, a bug can crash it on launch day, a big client can leave, or hackers can steal users' data.
businesses.tip: Mix steady client work with a few bets of your own, so one flop can never sink the whole studio.

cases.title: The first big plan
cases.story: Your studio opens with six coders. A bank offers $60,000 to build its new banking app in four months. Your team would rather spend a whole year making one giant game of their own. What is your plan?

options.text: Take the bank job and let a small team build a little game too
options.result: The bank's money pays the salaries, and the little game teaches you what players enjoy. Steady work plus a small bet keeps the studio safe.
options.lesson: Steady paid work keeps the lights on while you test your own bigger ideas.

options.text: Hire a project manager to plan the work and talk to clients
options.result: Priya, your new project manager, splits the work into weekly goals. Deadlines are met and the bank is delighted, though her salary costs extra.
options.lesson: A good manager turns a group of clever people into a team that finishes on time.

options.text: Put the whole team on one giant game for a year
options.result: A year later the game is only half finished and the money is nearly gone. Nobody has played it yet, so you still do not know if it is fun.
options.lesson: Do not bet everything on one huge idea; test something small first and learn fast.

options.text: Promise the bank it will be ready in four weeks, to impress them
options.result: The bank is thrilled, but four weeks is impossible. The app is late and full of bugs, and the bank tells other companies about it.
options.lesson: Promise only what your team can really deliver; a broken promise costs more than a lost deal.

options.text: Copy a famous game, change its name and sell it fast
options.result: The famous game's makers spot the copy within a week. The app store removes it, and their lawyers make you pay for using their work.
options.lesson: Copying someone else's work is stealing, and it is very easy to get caught.

cases.title: A hacker got in
cases.story: Your homework app has 80,000 users. A hacker guessed a coder's password, 'password123', and copied users' email addresses. Nobody outside the studio knows yet. What do you do?

options.text: Tell users and the data protection office today, and fix the hole
options.result: Some users are upset, but they thank you for being quick and honest. The hole is closed the same day, and most families keep using the app.
options.lesson: Owning up fast and fixing the problem keeps people's trust, even after a mistake.

options.text: Turn on two-step login and long passwords for every account
options.result: Now a stolen password is not enough: every login also needs a code sent to a phone. The next hacker who tries gives up.
options.lesson: Strong passwords and two-step login lock the door that hackers try first.

options.text: Pay a security expert to test the whole app for weak spots
options.result: The expert finds three more weak spots and you fix them all. It is expensive, but the app is much safer now.
options.lesson: Paying an expert to find holes costs less than letting a criminal find them.

options.text: Fire the coder in front of everyone to show you are tough
options.result: The team is frightened and two more coders quit. The real problem was that nobody had ever been taught safe passwords.
options.lesson: Fix the system that allowed a mistake instead of scaring the whole team.

options.text: Keep it secret, so users do not panic and delete the app
options.result: Weeks later a reporter finds out. Hiding a data leak is against the law, so you pay a big fine, and angry parents delete the app.
options.lesson: Hiding a data leak turns one problem into two: the leak and the cover-up.

cases.title: Money comes knocking
cases.story: Your puzzle game is a hit with 2 million players! An investor offers $400,000 to own a quarter of the studio. And an online 'adviser' promises to turn $40,000 of your profit into $1 million in one month.

options.text: Take the investor's money after your lawyer checks the deal
options.result: Your lawyer makes sure you stay in charge. The $400,000 pays for new coders and a safety cushion, so one flop can no longer sink you.
options.lesson: Sharing a slice of a growing company can make the whole company stronger and safer.

options.text: Use the hit's profits to build a second game, step by step
options.result: The second game grows slowly but surely. With two games earning, the studio no longer depends on one hit.
options.lesson: Two earners are safer than one: hits fade, so start the next one early.

options.text: Translate the game into five languages for new countries
options.result: Players in Brazil, Japan and Poland discover your puzzles. Downloads keep climbing for months.
options.lesson: A product people already love can find new fans in new markets.

options.text: Spend every dollar of profit on giant adverts this month
options.result: Downloads jump for a few weeks, then fall back. The adverts cost far more than the new players spent.
options.lesson: Big spending on a short burst rarely pays; check what each new customer is worth.

options.text: Send $40,000 to the adviser: a million dollars in a month!
options.result: The 'adviser' and your $40,000 vanish. Nobody can make money grow 25 times in a month; it was a scam all along.
options.lesson: Huge, sure profits in a hurry are always a scam; real investing grows slowly.

businesses.pitch: A busy Italian restaurant where families come for pasta, pizza and puddings.
businesses.earns: Each meal sells for about three times what its ingredients cost, and busy evenings and holidays fill every table.
businesses.costs: Chefs' and waiters' wages, fresh food, rent for the building, gas and electricity, and replacing broken plates.
businesses.risks: Quiet weeks, a bad review, a food-safety mistake, a new restaurant opening next door, or your best chef leaving.
businesses.tip: Keep the menu short and the kitchen spotless; happy regulars bring their friends, and that advertising is free.

cases.title: Who runs the kitchen?
cases.story: Your 60-seat restaurant opens in two weeks. Marco, an experienced head chef (the boss of the kitchen), asks $4,000 a month. You also need your first customers fast. What will you do?

options.text: Hire Marco at fair pay and plan the menu together
options.result: Marco builds a short menu of dishes his team can cook perfectly every time. Plates come out hot and fast, and word spreads: the tables fill up.
options.lesson: Paying fairly for a skilled leader is an investment, not a waste.

options.text: Hold a test night for friends and family before opening
options.result: The test night shows that the pizza oven is too slow for a full room. You fix it before the real opening, so paying diners never notice.
options.lesson: Practise on a friendly crowd first, and fix the problems before real customers arrive.

options.text: Give free starters to nearby office workers during opening week
options.result: Lunchtimes are packed for a few weeks and some workers come back with their families. Later the free-food crowd fades away.
options.lesson: A free taste brings people in, but only good food brings them back.

options.text: Put 50 dishes on the menu so everyone finds something
options.result: The kitchen needs so many ingredients that lots of them go off before they are used. Orders are slow and the food is only so-so.
options.lesson: A short menu done brilliantly beats a long menu done badly.

options.text: Buy 200 five-star reviews online for just $300
options.result: The review website spots the fakes and warns diners that you bought them. Inspectors fine you for fooling customers.
options.lesson: Fake reviews trick customers, and when they are found out, nobody trusts you.

cases.title: A food-safety scare
cases.story: Three diners say they felt ill after eating your chicken on Saturday. The kitchen fridge may have been too warm overnight. A food inspector visits on Friday. What do you do?

options.text: Close for a day, deep clean, check every fridge and tell diners
options.result: You find the broken fridge, throw out the risky food and explain everything on your website. The inspector praises your honesty and your clean kitchen.
options.lesson: In a crisis, find the cause, fix it and tell people the truth: that is how trust survives.

options.text: Phone the three diners, say sorry and refund their meals
options.result: The diners are surprised and pleased that the owner called them personally. One even books a table for next month.
options.lesson: A quick, sincere sorry can turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one.

options.text: Fit fridge alarms that text the chef if they get too warm
options.result: Two months later an alarm wakes the chef at 3am: a fridge door was left open. The food is saved and nobody gets ill.
options.lesson: Simple safety tools catch small problems before they become big ones.

options.text: Post online that the diners are making it up
options.result: Your post is shared everywhere, and people are shocked that you blamed ill customers. Bookings drop sharply.
options.lesson: Attacking unhappy customers in public always makes a problem bigger.

options.text: Throw away the fridge temperature log before the inspector comes
options.result: The inspector asks for the log and sees it is missing. Hiding evidence makes it far worse: a big fine and a low food hygiene score on your door.
options.lesson: Hiding a problem from inspectors and customers turns a mistake into a scandal.

cases.title: Ten more restaurants?
cases.story: Zest Foods wants to open ten copies of your restaurant in other towns, using your name and recipes (that is a franchise). They would pay you $1,000 a month for each one, but say: sign tonight or the offer is gone.

options.text: Ask a lawyer to read every page, then agree with quality rules
options.result: The lawyer finds that Zest could change your recipes, so you add quality rules and the right to inspect. The fees soon arrive every month.
options.lesson: Read a contract carefully before you sign; the small print is where the surprises hide.

options.text: Start with two restaurants as a trial before agreeing to ten
options.result: The two trial restaurants go well, so you agree to more. Testing first means you never put your good name at risk all at once.
options.lesson: Try a big step on a small scale first; it is cheaper to learn from a small mistake.

options.text: Negotiate a higher fee for each restaurant before agreeing
options.result: Zest really wants your recipes, so they agree to $1,300 a month for each restaurant. Asking politely earned you more every single month.
options.lesson: When someone wants what you have, it is fair to ask for a better price.

options.text: Open a second restaurant of your own, slowly
options.result: Your second restaurant is lovely but costs a lot to set up. It takes many months before it earns back the money.
options.lesson: Growing on your own keeps control, but it is slower and needs more of your money.

options.text: Sign tonight before the offer disappears
options.result: The small print lets Zest sell cheap frozen meals under your name and pay you nothing for five years. Diners blame you for their bad food.
options.lesson: 'Sign tonight or lose it' is a warning sign; a good deal will still be there tomorrow.

businesses.pitch: Electric scooters that people unlock with a phone app and ride around the city.
businesses.earns: Riders pay $1 to unlock a scooter and 20 cents a minute; sunny days and busy streets mean thousands of rides.
businesses.costs: Buying and charging scooters, repairs, staff who collect and fix them, insurance, and a fee to the city council.
businesses.risks: Rainy months, accidents, scooters left blocking pavements, broken scooters, a rival company, or a council ban.
businesses.tip: Safety first: riders, walkers and the council must all trust you, or the city can switch you off overnight.

cases.title: 300 scooters arrive
cases.story: Your 300 scooters arrive next week. The council will let you run them if riders are safe and scooters do not block pavements. What will you set up first?

options.text: Use GPS to slow scooters near schools and mark parking bays
options.result: GPS (the scooter knows where it is) slows riders in busy places, and neat parking bays keep pavements clear. The council and riders are both happy.
options.lesson: Building safety into your product wins the trust you need to grow.

options.text: Hire a team to charge and check every scooter each night
options.result: Every morning the scooters are full of charge and safe to ride. The team costs money, but riders never find a flat or broken scooter.
options.lesson: Riders come back when your product works every single time.

options.text: Add a quick safety quiz in the app before anyone's first ride
options.result: New riders learn the rules in one minute: no pavements, one person per scooter, park in a bay. There are fewer bumps and complaints.
options.lesson: Teaching customers the rules is cheap and makes everyone safer.

options.text: Put all 300 scooters in the city centre where the crowds are
options.result: Rides shoot up, but scooters pile up on busy pavements and people complain. The council sends you a warning letter.
options.lesson: Chasing the biggest crowd is not enough; think about the people around your business too.

options.text: Skip insurance to save $2,000 a month
options.result: You save a little each month, but now one bad crash could cost you a fortune. The council's permit officer is not impressed.
options.lesson: Insurance feels like wasted money until the day you really need it.

cases.title: A brake fails
cases.story: A rider fell when a scooter's brake failed. She sprained her wrist and will be fine. Your mechanics say checking every brake each day takes too long, and the council wants answers by Monday.

options.text: Check every brake before scooters go out again, and tell the council
options.result: You find twelve worn brakes and fix them all. Your honest report shows the council you take safety seriously, so you are allowed to keep going.
options.lesson: Losing a few days of rides is a small price for safety and the city's trust.

options.text: Visit the rider, say sorry and pay for her treatment
options.result: The rider is grateful that you came in person. She tells the local newspaper that your company did the right thing.
options.lesson: When someone is hurt by your product, caring comes first and paperwork second.

options.text: Fit smart sensors that warn when a brake is wearing out
options.result: Now each scooter reports its own brakes to the mechanics' screens. It costs a lot, but worn brakes are spotted before they fail.
options.lesson: Good technology can make safety checks quicker without skipping them.

options.text: Say the rider must have been riding badly
options.result: The repair records show the brake was worn out. Blaming the rider makes you look careless and unkind.
options.lesson: Blaming a customer for your own fault makes people trust you even less.

options.text: Skip the daily brake checks to keep more scooters on the road
options.result: Another brake fails and a second rider is hurt. The council fines you and stops your scooters for a month. Saving time on safety cost far more.
options.lesson: Never cut a safety check to save time; accidents cost far more than checks.

cases.title: The big city contract
cases.story: The council will pick only two scooter companies to run the city for three years. Bids (written offers) are due next month. A man called Rex says he knows someone at the council and can make sure you win, for $20,000 in cash with no receipt.

options.text: Write an honest bid showing your safety record and parking plan
options.result: Your clear safety numbers impress the council and you win a three-year contract. Knowing you will stay for years, you can plan ahead with confidence.
options.lesson: Win big contracts by being the best choice, and show proof of it.

options.text: Team up with the bus company so riders can hop from bus to scooter
options.result: One ticket now covers the bus and the last part of the journey by scooter. People going to work love it, and the council likes the idea too.
options.lesson: A partner who serves the same customers can make both businesses stronger.

options.text: Offer free rides to nurses and carers on their way to work
options.result: Hospital staff thank you on the local radio. The free rides cost a little, but the whole city now sees you as a good neighbour.
options.lesson: Helping your community is right, and people remember who helped.

options.text: Bid a price so low you cannot afford it, just to win
options.result: You win, but every ride now loses money. After a few months you must ask the council to change the deal, and they are not pleased.
options.lesson: Winning a contract that loses money is not really winning.

options.text: Pay Rex the $20,000 in cash so you are sure to win
options.result: Rex was asking for a bribe, which is against the law. The council finds out, throws out your bid and fines you. The $20,000 is gone too.
options.lesson: Secret cash with no receipt to win a deal is a bribe: illegal and a trap.

businesses.pitch: A fleet of vans and drivers delivering parcels for online shops across the city.
businesses.earns: Shops pay you about $4 for every parcel you deliver, and at Christmas the vans carry twice as many.
businesses.costs: Drivers' wages, the vans, fuel or charging, a big warehouse, and the software that plans each route.
businesses.risks: Late parcels, a van crash, drivers leaving, fuel prices rising, or a big customer moving to a cheaper rival.
businesses.tip: Treat drivers well and plan smart routes: on-time parcels and happy drivers keep big customers loyal.

cases.title: The first big customer
cases.story: Your delivery company starts with 20 drivers, 20 vans and a warehouse. ShopRight, a big online shop, will send you 2,000 parcels a day if you deliver on time. How will you get ready?

options.text: Buy route-planning software that finds the quickest roads
options.result: The software plans each van's route around traffic. Drivers finish on time, use less fuel, and ShopRight's parcels arrive when promised.
options.lesson: Smart planning saves time and money on every single trip.

options.text: Train every driver in safe, careful driving
options.result: Fewer dents, fewer fines and calmer drivers. Smooth driving even uses less fuel, so the training pays for itself.
options.lesson: Training your team is one of the best investments a company can make.

options.text: Swap half the vans for electric ones that are cheap to charge
options.result: The electric vans cost a lot to buy but very little to run. Quiet, clean vans also help ShopRight tell its customers it cares about the planet.
options.lesson: Green choices can cost more today and save money for years.

options.text: Say yes to every shop that asks, even with only 20 vans
options.result: Parcels pile up in the warehouse and deliveries are days late. ShopRight warns that it will leave if it happens again.
options.lesson: Never promise more than you can deliver; it ruins your good name.

cases.title: Drivers at breaking point
cases.story: It is nearly Christmas and parcels have doubled. Drivers say their routes are impossible to finish, two have quit, and the rest have asked for a meeting. What do you do?

options.text: Meet the drivers, listen, and set fair routes with proper breaks
options.result: The drivers point out three routes that cross the whole city twice. You fix them together, nobody else quits, and parcels arrive on time again.
options.lesson: Listen to the people doing the work; they often know the answer already.

options.text: Hire extra drivers just for the Christmas rush
options.result: Ten extra drivers share the load until January. It costs more, but every parcel arrives in time for Christmas.
options.lesson: Plan extra help for your busiest season instead of overloading your team.

options.text: Pay a Christmas bonus to every driver who stays
options.result: The drivers feel valued and stay for the rush. Keeping experienced drivers is cheaper than training new ones.
options.lesson: Showing staff they are valued keeps your best people.

options.text: Tell them anyone who complains can find another job
options.result: Five more drivers leave the next day. Parcels pile up, and hiring and training new drivers costs a fortune.
options.lesson: A boss who will not listen soon has nobody left to lead.

options.text: Pay drivers $100 extra to skip their rest breaks this month
options.result: Tired drivers make mistakes: one van scrapes three parked cars. Drivers must rest by law, so the road safety office fines you too.
options.lesson: Tired drivers are dangerous drivers; rest breaks are a safety rule, not a luxury.

cases.title: A double-sized contract?
cases.story: An email that looks like it is from ShopRight says: 'Great news! We want to double your contract. Log in at this link with your company password to sign today.' It comes from shopright-deals.net, not shopright.com.

options.text: Phone your contact at ShopRight on the number you already have
options.result: ShopRight never sent it: it was phishing (a fake email that steals passwords). Impressed by your care, they really do give you more parcels next year.
options.lesson: Check a surprising email by phoning a number you already trust, never by its link.

options.text: Report the fake email and teach staff how to spot others
options.result: A week later the same trick arrives for your accounts team. They recognise it at once and delete it.
options.lesson: One person who spots a scam can protect the whole company if they share it.

options.text: Just delete the email
options.result: You are safe this time, but nobody else is warned, and next week a new driver almost clicks a similar link.
options.lesson: Avoiding a scam is good; warning your team is even better.

options.text: Reply to the email and ask if it is really from ShopRight
options.result: The scammers answer 'Yes, it is real!' and send another link. Asking a stranger to check themselves proves nothing.
options.lesson: Never ask a suspicious sender to prove who they are; check another way.

options.text: Click the link and log in quickly before the offer goes
options.result: The link opens a fake page. Criminals use your password to move $75,000 of company money into their own account.
options.lesson: Never type a company password into a link from an email, however exciting it looks.

businesses.pitch: A big supermarket selling food and everyday things to thousands of local families.
businesses.earns: It makes only a few cents on each item, but sells so many thousands every day that it adds up to steady profits.
businesses.costs: Buying stock from suppliers, staff wages, rent, fridges and freezers running all day, and food that goes out of date.
businesses.risks: A cheaper rival chain, a supplier letting you down, food going to waste, or shoplifting.
businesses.tip: Tiny profits on each item add up: buy well, waste little and keep shelves full of what customers want.

cases.title: Getting ready to open
cases.story: Your supermarket opens next month. A big supplier offers milk, bread and fruit at its normal price. Amara, your store manager, thinks you could get a better deal, and the old tills keep breaking. What will you do?

options.text: Negotiate: promise a year of orders in return for a lower price
options.result: The supplier agrees to 8% off in return for a year of steady orders. Every item now earns a little more, and your shelves are never empty.
options.lesson: Offer something the other side wants, and you can ask for a better price.

options.text: Put in new tills, including fast self-checkouts
options.result: Queues are shorter and the tills never break. They cost a lot, but customers notice how quick it is to pay.
options.lesson: Fixing what annoys customers every day is worth paying for.

options.text: Ask local families what they would like to find on the shelves
options.result: Families ask for more fresh bread, gluten-free food and spices from around the world. You stock them, and those shelves sell out first.
options.lesson: The quickest way to know what customers want is to ask them.

options.text: Price everything below every rival, even below what it costs you
options.result: The store is packed, but you lose money on almost every basket. You cannot keep it up for long.
options.lesson: Busy is not the same as profitable; every sale must earn something.

cases.title: The lorry is late
cases.story: A storm has closed the main road, so your fruit and vegetable lorry will be four days late. Shelves are emptying fast. A man offers 'top brand' crisps and chocolate at half price, cash only, from the back of his van.

options.text: Buy from two local farms to fill the gap, and keep them as backups
options.result: The farms deliver fresh apples and carrots the next morning. Now you have three suppliers, so one late lorry can never empty your shelves again.
options.lesson: Never depend on just one supplier; a backup keeps you open when things go wrong.

options.text: Put up honest signs explaining the delay and when fruit returns
options.result: Shoppers understand the storm is not your fault and thank you for telling them. Most come back on Friday for their fruit.
options.lesson: When something goes wrong, telling customers the truth keeps their trust.

options.text: Fill the gaps with frozen and tinned vegetables for now
options.result: Frozen peas and tinned tomatoes fly off the shelves. It is not the same as fresh food, but families can still cook dinner.
options.lesson: When one product runs out, offer the next best thing.

options.text: Double the price of the fruit you still have
options.result: You make a little extra this week, but shoppers feel cheated and some move to the rival supermarket for good.
options.lesson: Raising prices when customers have no choice feels unfair, and they remember it.

options.text: Buy the van man's half-price 'top brand' snacks for cash
options.result: The snacks are fakes in copied wrappers, and customers say they taste odd. Inspectors fine you for selling counterfeit (fake copied) goods.
options.lesson: Famous brands at half price, cash only, from a van are almost always fakes.

cases.title: The loyalty card data
cases.story: Your loyalty card (members collect points every time they shop) has 20,000 members. An advertising company offers $50,000 for the members' names, addresses and lists of what they buy. What will you do?

options.text: Keep the data private and use the points to reward your regulars
options.result: Members get birthday treats and points on the things they buy most. They feel looked after, and they keep shopping with you even when times are hard.
options.lesson: Use customers' data to serve them better, never to sell them out.

options.text: Share data only with members who say yes to partner offers
options.result: You ask every member clearly. About a quarter say yes, and they enjoy the offers. Everyone else's data stays private.
options.lesson: Asking clear permission first is what makes sharing data fair.

options.text: Turn the card into a phone app with digital coupons
options.result: Younger shoppers love the app, and some order online for collection. It takes a while for older members to try it.
options.lesson: Meet customers where they are, on their phones as well as in the shop.

options.text: Give every member double points forever
options.result: Members are thrilled, but every point costs you money. Your thin profit on each item almost disappears.
options.lesson: A reward you cannot afford forever is a promise you will have to break.

options.text: Sell the members' details to the advertisers for easy money
options.result: Members start getting strange adverts and calls and work out where they came from. Selling data without permission breaks the law: a huge fine.
options.lesson: Customers' data belongs to them; never sell it without their clear permission.

businesses.pitch: An indoor farm that grows salad and herbs on tall shelves under LED lights.
businesses.earns: Supermarkets and restaurants pay well for fresh, local leaves picked the same morning, every month of the year.
businesses.costs: Electricity for the lights, water pumps, seeds, workers, and expensive machines that control heat and light.
businesses.risks: Electricity prices jumping, a plant disease spreading through the shelves, a pump breaking, or a big buyer leaving.
businesses.tip: Sell to several buyers and keep energy costs low; a farm that relies on one customer or cheap power is fragile.

cases.title: Who buys the first crop?
cases.story: Your farm's ten floors of shelves are ready. FreshMart would buy lots of lettuce every week at a low price. Chef Ines wants herbs for her three restaurants at a high price, but only a few boxes a week. How will you start?

options.text: Sell lettuce to FreshMart and herbs to Chef Ines: two kinds of buyer
options.result: FreshMart's steady order pays the bills, and the pricey herbs add extra profit. If one buyer leaves, the other still keeps you going.
options.lesson: Several customers are safer than one, however big that one is.

options.text: Start with three floors, learn what grows best, then fill the rest
options.result: In the first month you find that basil grows twice as fast as lettuce under your lights. You fill the other floors with what works.
options.lesson: Start small, learn quickly, then grow what works.

options.text: Fit sensors that give each plant exactly the light and water it needs
options.result: The sensors cost a lot, but no plant gets too much water or light. Leaves grow faster and the power bill drops.
options.lesson: Technology pays when it saves you money every single day.

options.text: Hire Dr Okafor, a plant scientist, as your farm manager
options.result: Dr Okafor knows exactly why leaves turn yellow and how to stop it. Her salary is high, so it takes a while before she pays for herself.
options.lesson: Expert help costs money; it pays off most when the problem is hard.

options.text: Grow 40 different rare plants to impress everyone
options.result: Every plant needs different light and care, and most rare plants have no buyer yet. Many crops end up in the compost bin.
options.lesson: Grow what customers will buy, not just what looks exciting.

cases.title: The power bill triples
cases.story: Electricity prices have tripled this winter. Your lights shine 16 hours a day, so the monthly power bill has jumped from $12,000 to $36,000. What do you do?

options.text: Fit low-energy lights and run them at night, when power is cheaper
options.result: The new lights use half the power, and night-time electricity is cheaper. The plants do not mind, and the bill drops to $15,000.
options.lesson: Know your biggest cost and tackle it first.

options.text: Explain the rise to buyers and add 10 cents to each bag
options.result: Your buyers know power prices have soared. Most accept the small rise, because fresh local salad is still worth it.
options.lesson: When your costs really rise, a small, honest price rise is fair.

options.text: Fix your electricity price for two years with a power company
options.result: The fixed price is not cheap, but now it cannot jump again. You can plan the next two years without nasty surprises.
options.lesson: A fixed price protects you from shocks, so you can plan ahead.

options.text: Turn the lights down by half to save power
options.result: The bill falls, but the plants grow half as fast. You cannot fill your orders, and FreshMart is unhappy.
options.lesson: Cutting the very thing that makes your product is not saving; it is shrinking.

options.text: Buy a salesman's $50,000 box that 'cuts any power bill by 90%'
options.result: The box is just lights and plastic. The bill does not change, the salesman stops answering his phone, and your $50,000 is gone.
options.lesson: If a gadget promises a miracle, ask real customers for proof before you pay.

cases.title: A greener label
cases.story: A supermarket chain will pay 20% more for salad with a proper green label, in all 50 of its shops. Solar panels for your roof would cost $150,000. Your marketing assistant says: 'Just print organic on the bags. We have no certificate, but who checks?'

options.text: Fit solar panels and show buyers your true green numbers
options.result: The panels make a third of your power for free. With real numbers to show, the chain gives you the green label and the higher price.
options.lesson: Real green changes can save money and win customers for years.

options.text: Turn leftover roots and leaves into compost for local gardens
options.result: Nothing goes to waste any more, and the bin bill shrinks. Local gardeners love the free compost and tell their friends.
options.lesson: Waste is often something useful that nobody has used yet.

options.text: Swap plastic boxes for paper bags that can be recycled
options.result: Shoppers like the paper bags, though the leaves wilt a little faster in them. It is a small step in the right direction.
options.lesson: Small green steps count, but check they work for your product too.

options.text: Ignore the label: shoppers only care about price
options.result: The chain picks a rival farm with a real green label. You keep your old price, but miss the biggest order of the year.
options.lesson: More and more customers care about the planet; ignoring them leaves money behind.

options.text: Print 'organic' on the bags: it costs nothing and sells more
options.result: Food inspectors do check. With no certificate, you must take every bag off the shelves and pay a fine, and the news calls it fake green.
options.lesson: Only claim what is true; customers and inspectors find out about fake labels.

businesses.pitch: A cinema with five screens showing the latest films, plus popcorn, snacks and drinks.
businesses.earns: Tickets bring in money, but most profit comes from popcorn and drinks; school holidays and big new films fill the seats.
businesses.costs: Film studios take about half of every ticket, plus staff wages, rent, electricity and keeping the projectors working.
businesses.risks: A run of boring films, people watching at home instead, a rival cinema opening, or a projector breaking on a big night.
businesses.tip: Give people a night out they cannot get at home: comfy seats, great sound and friendly staff.

cases.title: Opening night plans
cases.story: Your five-screen cinema is ready to open. Tickets in town cost about $12. Many people now watch films at home on the sofa, so you need reasons for them to come out. What will you do first?

options.text: Sell a $15-a-month card that lets members see as many films as they like
options.result: Hundreds of film fans sign up. The cards bring in steady money every month, and members buy popcorn every time they come.
options.lesson: Regular monthly customers keep your income steady, even in quiet weeks.

options.text: Fit big comfy seats and great sound in your two biggest screens
options.result: People say it feels better than any sofa. Those two screens sell out first every weekend, even at a slightly higher price.
options.lesson: Give customers an experience they cannot get at home.

options.text: Run cheap Saturday morning shows for families with little children
options.result: Parents love a calm, cheap morning out, with softer sound and the lights a little brighter. Many come back for birthday parties too.
options.lesson: Serving a group that others ignore can bring you loyal customers.

options.text: Charge $20 a ticket, because new films are popular
options.result: Most people decide to wait and watch the film at home. Half your seats stay empty on the opening weekend.
options.lesson: A price far above everyone else's needs a very good reason, or customers stay away.

cases.title: A giant rival opens
cases.story: A huge 20-screen cinema opens across town with $6 tickets. Your weekday crowds have halved, and your staff are worried about their jobs. What do you do?

options.text: Hold special nights: film quizzes, sing-alongs and birthday parties
options.result: Your cinema becomes the place for fun nights out, not just cheap tickets. The sing-along nights sell out weeks ahead.
options.lesson: When a rival is cheaper, be different and better, not just cheaper.

options.text: Ask your regulars what would keep them coming back
options.result: They ask for a quiet film club, cheaper snacks for children and easier parking. You do all three, and most of them stay.
options.lesson: Your loyal customers can tell you exactly how to keep them.

options.text: Cut prices on quiet weekday afternoons only
options.result: Students and retired people fill the afternoon shows. Evenings stay at the normal price, so you do not lose money.
options.lesson: Lower prices only when the seats would otherwise be empty.

options.text: Cut every ticket to $5 to beat them
options.result: The giant rival cuts to $4. Now both cinemas lose money, and they have far more cash than you to keep on fighting.
options.lesson: A price war with a much bigger rival is a fight you will probably lose.

options.text: Squeeze 40 more seats into each screen, in front of a side exit
options.result: A fire inspector finds the blocked exits and shuts the cinema until they are cleared, with a big fine. In an emergency, people need every exit.
options.lesson: Fire exits must always stay clear; no extra profit is worth people's safety.

cases.title: Empty morning seats
cases.story: Your screens sit empty on weekday mornings. The city's schools want to bring 5,000 pupils a year for film mornings at a special price. And a man offers you brand-new films a week before other cinemas, for $5,000 cash and no paperwork.

options.text: Agree a fair school price that fills the empty morning seats
options.result: Empty seats now earn money every weekday morning. Pupils love it, and many come back at the weekend with their families.
options.lesson: Selling empty seats cheaply is smart when they would otherwise earn nothing.

options.text: Add a teachers' guide and a short talk about how films are made
options.result: Teachers can now link the trip to their lessons, so more schools sign up every term.
options.lesson: Make your product fit what the customer really needs.

options.text: Rent empty screens to companies for big meetings
options.result: Companies love presenting on a giant screen with great sound. It is a brand-new way to earn from rooms you already have.
options.lesson: Look for new customers who could use what you already own.

options.text: Charge schools full adult prices: they have no other cinema nearby
options.result: The schools decide the trip is too expensive and stay at school instead. The seats stay empty and you earn nothing.
options.lesson: An empty seat earns nothing; a fair deal beats no deal.

options.text: Pay the man $5,000 cash for the early films and beat every rival
options.result: The films were stolen copies. The studios find out, stop sending you films and take you to court. Your $5,000 is lost too.
options.lesson: Cheap 'exclusive' deals for cash with no paperwork are usually stolen or fake.

businesses.pitch: A factory that designs and makes toys, from wooden trains to soft teddy bears.
businesses.earns: Toy shops and online stores buy your toys by the boxful; half the year's sales happen in the weeks before Christmas.
businesses.costs: Wood, plastic and fabric, factory workers' wages, machines, safety testing, and shipping toys to the shops.
businesses.risks: A toy nobody wants, a safety recall (calling unsafe toys back), a big shop cancelling an order, or missing Christmas.
businesses.tip: Test every toy as if your own little brother or sister will play with it; one unsafe toy can ruin a brand.

cases.title: 50,000 teddy bears
cases.story: ToyWorld, a chain of 200 shops, wants 50,000 teddy bears by October at $6 each: $300,000! Each bear costs you $4 to make, and you must buy all the fabric first. How do you handle your first giant order?

options.text: Say yes, but ask for a third of the money up front for materials
options.result: ToyWorld agrees to pay $100,000 now. You buy the fabric without borrowing, and the bears arrive on time.
options.lesson: Big orders need money before they pay; ask for a deposit (part of the money up front).

options.text: Hire extra workers on fair pay for the busy months
options.result: With the extra team, every order is finished without exhausted workers. Nobody has to stay late every night.
options.lesson: Plan extra help for busy times instead of wearing out your team.

options.text: Read the contract: what happens if you are a week late?
options.result: The small print says you pay $10,000 for every day late! You ask for a fairer $1,000 a day, and ToyWorld agrees.
options.lesson: Before you sign, read what happens if things go wrong.

options.text: Use cheaper, thinner fabric to earn more on each bear
options.result: The bears look worn out after one wash. Parents complain, and ToyWorld gives next year's order to another factory.
options.lesson: Saving a few cents on quality can cost you your best customer.

cases.title: The paint test
cases.story: It is October, and 20,000 toy trains must reach the shops for Christmas. The safety lab needs two weeks to test the new paint. Your paint supplier says: 'It is fine, I promise. Skip the test and ship now.'

options.text: Wait for the test, and tell the shops honestly about the delay
options.result: The test finds the paint flakes off when chewed! You switch to a safe paint and warn the shops. The trains arrive a week late, but safe.
options.lesson: Never skip a safety test on a child's toy; a short delay beats a dangerous toy.

options.text: Pay workers fair overtime to catch up once the test is done
options.result: Workers who want extra hours stay some evenings for extra pay, and the lost week is caught up. Nobody is forced to stay.
options.lesson: Ask, do not force: fair pay for extra work keeps your team on your side.

options.text: Send the toys that already passed their tests first
options.result: Teddy bears and puzzles reach the shops first, so the shelves stay full while the trains finish testing.
options.lesson: When one product is held up, keep the others moving.

options.text: Cancel the trains completely to avoid any risk
options.result: The shops are left with empty spaces at Christmas and are cross. Waiting two weeks would have saved the whole order.
options.lesson: Being careful does not mean giving up; find the safe way to go on.

options.text: Skip the test and ship now: the supplier promised it is fine
options.result: The paint flakes off when toddlers chew it. Every train must be recalled from shops and homes, and the fines and refunds are enormous.
options.lesson: A supplier's promise is not a safety test; check every toy made for children.

cases.title: Twice as many toys
cases.story: ToyWorld wants twice as many toys next year. A new production line (another row of machines) in your factory would cost about $100,000. A company abroad offers to make your toys for half your cost, but will not let you visit its factory.

options.text: Choose a maker that lets you visit and treats its workers fairly
options.result: You find a fair factory in Portugal that welcomes visitors. Costs fall, quality is good, and you can tell shops proudly how your toys are made.
options.lesson: Know who makes your products and how they are treated; your name is on every box.

options.text: Build the new production line in your own factory
options.result: The new line costs a lot, but you control every step. The town gains new jobs and is proud of its toy factory.
options.lesson: Keeping control of quality can be worth paying a bit more.

options.text: Ask ToyWorld to sign a two-year order before you spend anything
options.result: ToyWorld signs for two years. Now you know the extra toys will really be sold before you invest in making them.
options.lesson: Get the order promised in writing before you spend big money to fill it.

options.text: Double everyone's hours for a year instead of hiring
options.result: Tired workers make mistakes, and several leave for calmer jobs. Overtime pay costs more than new staff would have.
options.lesson: Worn-out teams make mistakes; grow your team when the work grows.

options.text: Sign with the half-price factory abroad: no visit needed
options.result: A news team films inside: workers there are paid almost nothing for 14-hour days. Shops pull your toys, and you pay back their orders.
options.lesson: If a supplier hides how it treats its workers, its cheap price has a hidden cost.

businesses.pitch: A stylish 40-room hotel in the city centre for tourists and business travellers.
businesses.earns: Guests pay about $150 a night for a room, plus breakfast, meeting rooms and events; summer fills every room.
businesses.costs: Cleaners, receptionists and chefs, laundry, energy, repairs, and fees to booking websites for each guest they send.
businesses.risks: Empty rooms in quiet months, bad online reviews, a burst pipe, or tourists choosing a new hotel down the road.
businesses.tip: Every guest can write a review that thousands will read, so make each stay feel special.

cases.title: Doors open in May
cases.story: Your 40-room hotel opens in May. Booking websites fill rooms fast but keep 18% of every booking. You also need a general manager to run the hotel day to day. What will you do?

options.text: Hire Leila, an experienced manager, and train staff to welcome guests
options.result: Leila trains every receptionist and cleaner to learn guests' names and fix problems fast. Reviews start saying 'the staff made our trip'.
options.lesson: Great service comes from a well-trained, well-led team.

options.text: Use booking websites at first, and build your own booking website too
options.result: The big websites bring your first guests. Many book their next stay on your own site, so you keep the whole room price.
options.lesson: Use big websites to be found, then build your own way to reach customers.

options.text: Insure the hotel against fire, floods and burst pipes
options.result: The insurance costs money every year. In November a frozen pipe floods three rooms, and the insurer pays for nearly all the repairs.
options.lesson: Insurance turns a disaster you cannot afford into a bill you can.

options.text: Spend a fortune on a marble lobby before the rooms are finished
options.result: The lobby is stunning, but the rooms still have old beds and weak showers. Guests spend most of their time in their rooms, so reviews are mixed.
options.lesson: Spend your money where customers spend their time.

options.text: Add a surprise $25 'hotel fee' in tiny print at checkout
options.result: Guests feel tricked and say so in their reviews. Booking websites hide your hotel, and inspectors make you refund every fee.
options.lesson: Show the full price up front; hidden fees turn happy guests into angry reviewers.

cases.title: A rainy summer
cases.story: It has rained all summer, and a shiny new hotel has opened down the road. In July only half of your 40 rooms are booked, and the hotel is losing money. What do you do?

options.text: Create rainy-day packages with local museums and restaurants
options.result: Guests get a room, museum tickets and dinner for one price. Travel websites love it, and bookings climb even on wet weekends.
options.lesson: When the weather turns against you, give customers a new reason to come.

options.text: Win weekday bookings from companies for meetings and training
options.result: Three local companies book your meeting room and bedrooms every week. Business guests come rain or shine.
options.lesson: Different kinds of customers make a business steadier in a bad season.

options.text: Lower prices for last-minute bookings on empty nights
options.result: Some empty rooms fill up with bargain hunters. It helps a little, but you earn less for each room.
options.lesson: A small price cut can fill empty rooms, but it will not fix a bad season alone.

options.text: Cut the cleaners' hours in half to save money
options.result: The rooms are not quite clean, and guests notice. Two reviews say 'dusty', and bookings fall even further.
options.lesson: Cutting what guests care about most makes a bad season worse.

cases.title: A pop star books in
cases.story: Pop star Nova wants your whole hotel for a week at triple the normal price, but 15 rooms are already booked by other guests. A magazine also offers $20,000 for secret photos of Nova in the hotel.

options.text: Give Nova the 25 free rooms and keep your promise to booked guests
options.result: Nova's team takes 25 rooms and loves how calm the hotel is. Your other guests keep their rooms, plus the fun of a famous neighbour.
options.lesson: Keep your promises to the customers you have, even when a bigger one comes along.

options.text: Keep Nova's visit secret to protect her and the other guests
options.result: Your staff promise not to tell anyone. Nova's week is peaceful, and her manager says they will come back every year.
options.lesson: Protecting a guest's privacy is part of great service.

options.text: Ask for a deposit and a signed contract before Nova arrives
options.result: Nova's team pays half up front. When they change plans and leave two days early, you are still paid.
options.lesson: For big bookings, get a deposit and the deal in writing.

options.text: Cancel the other guests' bookings: Nova pays triple
options.result: Fifteen families find their holiday cancelled at the last minute. Their furious reviews say you only care about money.
options.lesson: Breaking promises to ordinary customers costs more than a star's money brings.

options.text: Sell the magazine secret photos of Nova for $20,000
options.result: Nova's lawyers find out where the photos came from. You pay back far more than $20,000, and famous guests never book with you again.
options.lesson: Guests trust you with their privacy; selling it is wrong and very costly.

businesses.pitch: A ten-floor office building in the city centre, rented out to companies.
businesses.earns: Companies pay about $4,000 a month for each floor, on leases (rental contracts) that usually last several years.
businesses.costs: Repairs, cleaning, lifts, heating and cooling, insurance, a building manager, and property taxes.
businesses.risks: A tenant (a company that rents a floor) leaving, floors standing empty, or an old lift or boiler breaking down.
businesses.tip: Happy tenants stay for years: fix problems fast and keep the building modern, and the rent keeps flowing in.

cases.title: Ten empty floors
cases.story: You now own a ten-floor office building, but no tenants (companies that rent space) yet. TechCo offers to rent all ten floors for ten years at a low price. Lots of smaller companies want one or two floors each at a higher rent.

options.text: Rent to several different companies, each signing for three to five years
options.result: A bakery's head office, a design firm, a charity and seven others move in. If one ever leaves, the other floors still pay rent.
options.lesson: Many different tenants are safer than one giant one.

options.text: Offer TechCo four floors at a higher rent, instead of all ten
options.result: TechCo agrees to four floors at a better rent. They are a solid tenant, but no longer so big that losing them would sink you.
options.lesson: You can say yes to part of a deal and shape it to suit you.

options.text: Have a lawyer write clear contracts: who fixes what, and when rent rises
options.result: Every tenant knows the rules from day one. When a radiator breaks, nobody argues about who pays.
options.lesson: Clear contracts stop arguments before they start.

options.text: Let anyone move in who can pay the first month, with no checks
options.result: One new tenant stops paying after two months and takes ages to leave. A quick check would have shown they had done it before.
options.lesson: Check a new tenant's history before you hand over the keys.

cases.title: A big tenant may leave
cases.story: BrightBank rents three floors for $12,000 a month. They say they will leave when their rental contract (lease) ends in six months, because the building feels old: slow lifts, chilly offices and nowhere to park bikes.

options.text: Ask BrightBank what would make them stay, and fix the top problems
options.result: They want warmer offices and bike storage most of all. You fix both, they sign for five more years, and the other tenants love the changes too.
options.lesson: Keeping a good customer is cheaper than finding a new one.

options.text: Offer a small rent discount if they sign for five more years
options.result: BrightBank likes the offer. You earn a little less per month, but you are sure of $11,000 a month for five years.
options.lesson: A small discount for a long promise can be a smart trade.

options.text: Start looking for a new tenant now, just in case
options.result: Two companies come to look round. Whatever BrightBank decides, the floors will not stand empty for long.
options.lesson: Plan for the worst while working for the best.

options.text: Threaten to take BrightBank to court if they leave
options.result: Their lawyers point out that the lease lets them leave. Now they are leaving cross, and they tell other companies you are hard to deal with.
options.lesson: Threats will not keep a customer; a better offer might.

options.text: When they leave, keep their $24,000 deposit by blaming old marks
options.result: BrightBank shows photos from the day they moved in: the marks were already there. A court makes you repay everything, plus their costs.
options.lesson: A deposit is the tenant's money, held in case of damage; keep only what real damage costs.

cases.title: A greener building
cases.story: Companies now want greener offices, and your heating bill is $5,000 a month. Insulation (warm padding in the walls) and a heat pump (a very efficient heater) would cost $180,000 and halve it. A salesman offers 'free' solar panels if you sign his 25-year contract today.

options.text: Pay for insulation and a heat pump, and tell tenants about it
options.result: Heating bills halve, offices are cosier, and companies looking for green offices ask to move in. Over the years, the work pays for itself.
options.lesson: Think long term: spend now on things that keep paying you back for years.

options.text: Ask three companies for prices before choosing who does the work
options.result: The prices range from $150,000 to $240,000 for the same job. Comparing them saves you a fortune.
options.lesson: Always compare a few prices before a big job; they can be very different.

options.text: Add bike racks, showers and plants to make the offices nicer
options.result: Cyclists can now ride to work and shower before meetings. Tenants say the building feels fresh and modern.
options.lesson: Small touches that make people's day better help tenants stay.

options.text: Change nothing: the building has worked fine for 30 years
options.result: One by one, companies move to newer, greener buildings nearby. Empty floors earn nothing, and the heating bill keeps climbing.
options.lesson: What worked for the last 30 years may not work for the next ten; keep improving.

options.text: Sign today for the 'free' solar panels: nothing to pay!
options.result: The small print says you must buy his electricity at double the normal price for 25 years, with a huge fee to leave early.
options.lesson: 'Free' deals with long contracts hide their cost in the small print; read every line first.

businesses.pitch: A colourful kids' splash park with a splash pad, small slides and shallow pools.
businesses.earns: Entry tickets and family passes, plus ice lollies, snacks, party packages and school swim afternoons in summer.
businesses.costs: Lifeguards and gate staff, water and pool chemicals, pumps, parasols, insurance and repairs.
businesses.risks: Rainy or cold weeks, over-full hot days, a child getting hurt, dirty water, and a rival park with bigger slides.
businesses.tip: You sell safe, happy days for families: watch the water and the children first, and the profit follows.

cases.title: Who watches the water?
cases.story: Your splash park opens in three weeks with four shallow pools, all knee-deep. A lifeguard costs about $2,800 a month. A friend says: 'The water is so shallow that parents can watch their own children.'

options.text: Skip lifeguards: the water is shallow and parents are watching
options.result: On a busy day a toddler slips under unseen. A parent grabs her in seconds and she is fine, but the council shuts the park for a month and fines you.
options.lesson: Shallow water can still be dangerous: lifeguards are never a cost you cut.

options.text: Hire four trained lifeguards, one per pool, and train all staff in first aid
options.result: Whistles stay quiet because the lifeguards spot trouble early. Parents tell each other, 'It feels properly looked after,' and visits climb.
options.lesson: Safety costs money every month, and it is the reason families trust you.

options.text: Pay a pool-safety expert to check the pools before opening
options.result: The expert finds a drain cover that is a little loose and a slippery step. Both are fixed before a single child arrives.
options.lesson: A fresh pair of expert eyes sees what a busy boss misses.

options.text: Add clear rules: adults stay with under-8s, wristbands show a phone number
options.result: A little boy wanders off on day one, but his wristband gets him back to his dad in two minutes. Parents love the idea.
options.lesson: Simple rules and cheap tools make a safe place safer, but they never replace trained people.

options.text: Buy a giant bucket tower first and hire lifeguards later
options.result: The bucket tower looks great in photos, but the inspector will not let you open until lifeguards are hired. Opening day slips by a month.
options.lesson: Do the must-haves first, such as safety, and the fun extras second.

cases.title: Heatwave at the gate
cases.story: It is 36 degrees. The park is safe for 600 guests at once, but 1,400 people are queuing in the sun. Your cashier says: 'Let everyone in. Think of the money!'

options.text: Let everyone in: more guests, more money today
options.result: The pools are so packed that children cannot swim safely. Lifeguards blow whistles all day, and the health officer fines you.
options.lesson: A safe limit is a promise to every family already inside.

options.text: Keep the safe limit and text each family when their turn comes
options.result: Families wait in the shade of the park next door and come back when their phone buzzes. Nobody is squashed, and many buy lollies on the way in.
options.lesson: Say 'not yet' kindly and give people a way to wait, and they stay your customers.

options.text: Put shade, parasols and free water taps in the queue
options.result: The queue is still long, but nobody gets sunburnt or dizzy. Mums and dads say, 'At least they care about us.'
options.lesson: When customers must wait, make the wait safe and comfortable.

options.text: Sell timed tickets online for morning or afternoon slots
options.result: Families book ahead and arrive at their time slot. Queues shrink, and the quiet afternoons fill up too.
options.lesson: Spread busy days across the day with booking, and the same park earns more.

options.text: Charge $3 extra on the hottest days
options.result: Some families grumble, but the queue gets shorter and the money buys more shade. A few say it feels unfair.
options.lesson: Higher prices when it is busy can work, but explain them kindly.

cases.title: Passes, parties and a drinks deal
cases.story: A school wants swim afternoons on school days at $6 a child. Parents ask about birthday parties. A fizzy-drink company offers $20,000 a year if you sell only its drinks and remove the free water taps.

options.text: Sign the drinks deal and take out the free water taps
options.result: On a hot day children get thirsty and only fizzy drinks are left. The health officer orders the taps back, and you pay to fit them again.
options.lesson: Never sell away something people need for their health, not even for easy money.

options.text: Say yes to the school: swim afternoons on school days at $6 a child
options.result: Weekday afternoons were quiet anyway. Three schools book regular slots, and the children tell their parents, who come back at the weekend.
options.lesson: Fill your quiet times with a steady customer, and the busy times take care of themselves.

options.text: Add birthday party packages with a party host and a shady table
options.result: Every Saturday has two parties. The host sets up a cake table, and each birthday child invites a dozen new families.
options.lesson: A package that makes one special day easy can be worth much more than a ticket.

options.text: Sell a summer family pass: $100 for four, paid back after three visits
options.result: Two hundred families buy passes in May, so cash arrives early. Many come on average days when the park would be half empty.
options.lesson: Passes bring money in early and make families come back.

options.text: Cut all tickets to $5 for the whole summer so the park is always full
options.result: The park is full, but each ticket earns so little that the lifeguards and the water bill eat the profit.
options.lesson: A full park is not the goal: profit is. Check that each guest pays for what they cost you.
